articleHeader.title: Python RegEx — The re Module Explained Properly
articleHeader.subtitle: Everything you actually need to know about regular expressions in Python — the re module, match vs search vs findall, groups, special characters, raw strings, greedy vs lazy matching, and the mistakes every developer makes while learning this.

blocks.text: A regular expression — RegEx for short — is a tiny, specialised pattern language for describing shapes of text: 'a string that starts with three digits, then a hyphen, then four more digits' instead of 'exactly the string 123-4567'. Python gives you access to this pattern language through the built-in re module. re.search(r'\d{3}-\d{4}', text) finds a phone-number-shaped chunk of text anywhere inside text, without you writing a single line of manual character-by-character checking.

RegEx has a genuinely intimidating reputation, and honestly, some of that reputation is earned — a complex pattern like ^(?:[a-z0-9!#$%&'*+/=?^_\`{|}~-]+(?:\.[a-z0-9!#$%&'*+/=?^_\`{|}~-]+)*)@... looks like line noise to anyone, experienced or not. But the core ideas underneath that intimidating surface are genuinely small: a handful of special characters mean specific things, a few functions do the actual matching, and once those pieces click, most everyday patterns — validate an email format, extract all the numbers from a string, find every hashtag in a tweet — become genuinely quick to write.

Here's the mistake I see constantly, including from myself early on: reaching for regex when a plain string method would do the job more clearly. Checking if a string starts with "http" doesn't need re.match(r'^http', url) — url.startswith('http') says exactly the same thing in code any Python developer can read at a glance, no pattern-language knowledge required. Regex earns its place specifically when the thing you're matching has real structural variation — multiple possible formats, optional parts, repeated patterns — not for simple, fixed-string checks.

This guide covers the re module's core functions, the essential special characters, capturing groups, the crucial difference between greedy and lazy matching, why raw strings matter, and the specific mistakes — like forgetting to escape a literal dot — that produce patterns which look right but silently match the wrong thing.

sections.title: History — Regular Expressions and Python's re Module

blocks.text: Regular expressions themselves predate Python by decades, rooted in formal language theory. Python's specific implementation has its own, somewhat bumpy history worth knowing.

items.text: — Regular expressions originate from the work of mathematician Stephen Kleene on regular languages and finite automata theory, long before any computer implementation existed.

— Regular expressions became practically famous through Unix tools like grep, sed, and ed, and later through the Perl programming language, which built an entire reputation around expressive, powerful regex support baked directly into its syntax.
— Python's very earliest regex support came through a module simply called regex, using a different, less standardized syntax than what Python developers use today.

— The re module, implementing a Perl-influenced regex syntax, was introduced to standardize and modernize Python's pattern-matching capabilities, and the older regex module was eventually deprecated and removed entirely.

— The re module's core API remained stable through the Python 2 to 3 transition, though string handling changes (everything becoming Unicode by default) affected how regex patterns interacted with non-ASCII text.

— Ongoing refinements continued improving re module performance and adding minor convenience features, while the fundamental pattern syntax itself remained deliberately stable to avoid breaking the enormous amount of existing regex-dependent code.

— The re module remains the standard, built-in way to do regex in Python, though the third-party regex package (offering additional features like nested named groups and better Unicode property support) is genuinely popular for advanced use cases the standard library doesn't cover. For nearly all everyday tasks, though, re remains entirely sufficient.

sections.title: Key Characteristics of Python's re Module

blocks.text: Here are the 11 things worth knowing precisely about how Python's regex support actually works:

items.title: Built Into the Standard Library
items.text: import re gives you full regex support with zero extra installation — no pip install needed for the standard, everyday regex functionality most tasks require.

items.title: Core Functions Serve Different Purposes
items.text: re.match() checks the START of a string, re.search() finds the FIRST match anywhere, re.findall() returns ALL matches as a list, re.finditer() returns all matches as an iterator of Match objects, and re.sub() replaces matches.

items.title: Match Objects Hold Rich Information
items.text: A successful match returns a Match object, not just a boolean — .group() gets the matched text, .start()/.end() give its position, and .groups() returns captured subgroups.

items.title: Raw Strings Are the Convention
items.text: Pattern strings are almost always written with an r prefix — r'\d+' — to prevent Python's own string escaping (like \n becoming a newline) from interfering with regex's own use of backslashes.

items.title: Special Characters Carry Specific Meaning
items.text: Characters like . ^ $ * + ? { } [ ] \ | ( ) each have a reserved, specific meaning in regex syntax and must be escaped with a backslash to match them as literal characters.

items.title: Parentheses Create Capturing Groups
items.text: Wrapping part of a pattern in () captures that specific portion of the match separately, retrievable via .group(1), .group(2), and so on, or all at once via .groups().

items.title: Groups Can Be Named
items.text: (?P<year>\d{4}) creates a named capturing group, retrievable more readably via match.group('year') instead of a numbered index that's easy to lose track of in complex patterns.

items.title: Greedy by Default, Lazy on Demand
items.text: Quantifiers like * and + match as MUCH as possible by default (greedy). Adding a ? after them (*?, +?) makes them match as LITTLE as possible instead (lazy/non-greedy).

items.title: Patterns Can Be Pre-Compiled
items.text: re.compile(pattern) creates a reusable Pattern object, genuinely faster when the same pattern is applied repeatedly, such as inside a loop processing many lines of text.

items.title: Flags Modify Matching Behaviour
items.text: re.IGNORECASE (or re.I) makes matching case-insensitive, re.MULTILINE changes how ^ and $ behave across multiple lines, and re.DOTALL makes . match newline characters too, which it doesn't by default.

items.title: Unicode-Aware by Default
items.text: In Python 3, \w, \d, and similar character classes match Unicode letters and digits by default, not just ASCII — matching Devanagari or other non-Latin script text correctly without extra configuration.

sections.title: How Python Matches a Pattern Against Text — Flowchart

blocks.text: Choosing the wrong function — match() versus search() versus findall() — is one of the most common regex mistakes, precisely because they sound similar but behave meaningfully differently. Here's the decision path, plus what happens once a match is actually found.

Key insight: match() only ever looks at the very beginning of the string — if the pattern would match perfectly starting at character five instead of character zero, match() still returns None. This single distinction accounts for a genuinely large share of 'why isn't my regex working' confusion, since search() would find that exact same pattern without any trouble.

sections.title: How RegEx Actually Works — Special Characters, Groups, and Greedy vs Lazy

blocks.text: Three things separate someone who's copy-pasted a regex pattern from Stack Overflow from someone who can actually write and debug their own: knowing the core special-character vocabulary precisely, understanding exactly what capturing groups do, and knowing the difference between greedy and lazy matching — a distinction that silently produces wrong results far more often than it produces an outright error.
🎭 The Essential Special-Character Vocabulary

A small set of characters covers the overwhelming majority of everyday regex needs: . matches any single character except a newline; \d matches any digit; \w matches any word character (letters, digits, underscore); \s matches any whitespace; * means 'zero or more of the previous thing'; + means 'one or more'; ? means 'zero or one, i.e. optional'; {3} means 'exactly three'; {2,5} means 'between two and five'; ^ anchors to the start of the string; $ anchors to the end; and [abc] matches any single character from that set. Learning these roughly ten symbols covers a genuinely large share of the patterns you'll ever need to write.
🔡 Why Raw Strings Matter — And What Breaks Without Them

Python's regular strings already treat backslash as an escape character — '\n' is a newline, '\t' is a tab. Regex ALSO uses backslash for its own special sequences — \d for digit, \w for word character. Without the r prefix, Python processes the backslash first, before regex ever sees the string — '\d' isn't a recognised Python escape sequence, so Python actually leaves it alone in this specific case, but plenty of other sequences (\b for word boundary in regex collides directly with \b as Python's backspace character escape) genuinely break without the raw-string prefix. The safe, standard habit is simply always writing regex patterns as raw strings: r'\d+\s\w+', never '\d+\s\w+'.
👥 Capturing Groups — Pulling Out the Parts You Actually Want

A pattern like r'(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})' matches a full date like 2026-03-24, but the parentheses do something extra: they capture each piece separately. match.group(0) (or just match.group()) gives the whole match, match.group(1) gives the year, match.group(2) the month, match.group(3) the day. This is what turns regex from a yes/no matching tool into a genuine text-extraction tool — finding that a string contains a date is useful, but pulling out the year specifically to use elsewhere in your code is usually the actual goal.
🍽️ Greedy vs Lazy — The Silent Wrong-Answer Trap

This is the single most common source of a regex that runs without error but returns the wrong match. Given the text <b>bold</b> and <i>italic</i>, the pattern r'<.+>' doesn't match just <b> — because + is greedy by default, it grabs as much text as possible while still allowing the overall pattern to match, so it actually matches all the way from the first < to the very last > in the string: <b>bold</b> and <i>italic</i> in its entirety. Adding a ? after the quantifier — r'<.+?>' — makes it lazy, matching as little as possible instead, correctly stopping at the very first > it encounters and giving you just <b>.

Simple rule to remember: always write patterns as raw strings, use search() unless you specifically need to check the string's start, remember that + and * are greedy by default and add ? when you need the lazy version instead, and reach for named or numbered groups whenever you need to extract a specific piece of the match, not just confirm that it matched.

sections.title: Regex Support — Python vs Other Languages

blocks.text: Regular expressions are largely portable across languages — the core syntax is remarkably similar everywhere — but how each language exposes and integrates that syntax genuinely differs.

rows: Native syntax in the language itself?
Low for basic use, notoriously deep for advanced use

blocks.text: Here's my honestly opinionated take: I genuinely think Python made the right call NOT baking regex literal syntax directly into the language the way JavaScript and Perl do. JavaScript's /pattern/ literals are undeniably convenient to type, but they also make it easy to sprinkle dense, cryptic patterns directly into otherwise readable code without a second thought. Python's re.compile(r'...') approach costs you a couple of extra characters and forces regex to visually stand out as its own distinct, deliberate tool being reached for — which, given how quickly regex readability degrades past a certain complexity, is a small nudge toward using it more thoughtfully rather than reflexively.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Using RegEx

blocks.text: Regex is a genuinely powerful tool for the right problems, and a genuine liability when reached for out of habit rather than necessity.

pros.title: Extremely Compact for Complex Patterns
pros.text: A single line of regex can express matching logic that would take dozens of lines of manual character-by-character string parsing to replicate.

pros.title: Genuinely Portable Across Languages
pros.text: Core regex syntax transfers almost directly between Python, JavaScript, Java, and most other languages — learning it once pays off broadly, not just within Python.

pros.title: Excellent for Text Extraction, Not Just Validation
pros.text: Capturing groups turn regex from a simple yes/no check into a genuine data-extraction tool, pulling structured pieces out of unstructured or semi-structured text.

pros.title: Built Into the Standard Library
pros.text: No external dependency is needed for the vast majority of regex tasks — import re is available in every standard Python installation.

pros.title: Fast for Repeated Matching When Compiled
pros.text: re.compile() lets a pattern be parsed once and reused many times, which matters genuinely when processing large volumes of text, like log files or scraped web content.

pros.title: Handles Structural Variation Elegantly
pros.text: Patterns with optional parts, alternatives, and repetition (phone numbers with or without a country code, for instance) are exactly where regex clearly outperforms manual string-method chains.

cons.title: Readability Degrades Quickly With Complexity
cons.text: A moderately complex pattern is genuinely hard for anyone — including its original author, months later — to read and modify confidently without careful, deliberate effort.

cons.title: Easy to Write a Pattern That's Subtly Wrong
cons.text: Forgetting to escape a literal dot, forgetting a raw string prefix, or missing a greedy-vs-lazy distinction produces patterns that run without error but silently match the wrong thing.

cons.title: Not the Right Tool for Truly Structured Formats
cons.text: Parsing genuine HTML, XML, or JSON with regex is a well-known anti-pattern — these formats have nested, recursive structure that regex fundamentally isn't designed to handle reliably; use a real parser instead.

cons.title: Can Be Genuinely Slow on Pathological Patterns
cons.text: Certain poorly constructed patterns can trigger catastrophic backtracking, where matching time explodes exponentially on specific unfortunate input — a real, documented performance and security concern (ReDoS).

cons.title: Overused for Simple String Checks
cons.text: Reaching for regex to check if a string starts with a fixed prefix, or contains a fixed substring, is unnecessary complexity when str.startswith() or the in operator says the same thing far more clearly.

cons.title: Debugging Requires Specialised Tooling or Practice
cons.text: Understanding exactly why a pattern isn't matching often requires stepping through it mentally, character by character, or using an external regex-testing tool — it's not always obvious from reading the pattern alone.

blocks.text: Practice This Code — Live Editor

blocks.initialCode:
import re

text = "Call 9876543210 or 8765432109 for support."
numbers = re.findall(r'\d{10}', text)
print(numbers)

blocks.text: Line-by-Line Explanation

items.html: r'[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+' — A simplified email pattern: one or more word/dot/plus/hyphen characters, an @, then a domain name, a literal dot (escaped as \.), and the extension. Real email validation is genuinely more complex than this, but this covers the common cases.
match.start() and match.end() — Give the exact character positions where the match begins and ends within the original string, useful for slicing or reporting exactly where something was found.
(?P<year>\d{4}) — A named capturing group. match.group('year') reads far more clearly in later code than a numbered match.group(1), especially in patterns with several groups.

r'<.+>' vs r'<.+?>' — The only difference is the ? after +. Without it, greedy matching grabs from the first < to the very LAST > in the whole string. With it, lazy matching stops at the very FIRST > it finds.

re.sub(r'<[^>]+>', '', html) — Uses a character class [^>] (meaning 'any character that is NOT >') instead of lazy matching to achieve a similar precise effect — a common, genuinely reliable alternative approach to the greedy-matching trap.

sections.title: Where RegEx Actually Earns Its Place — Real-World Applications

blocks.text: Regex isn't just an interview-question topic — it's genuinely embedded in a wide range of everyday Python tasks:

items.text: — Checking that a phone number, postal code, or username matches an expected format is one of the most common practical regex uses, especially in web backend request validation.

— Extracting timestamps, error codes, IP addresses, or specific message patterns from server log files is a textbook regex use case, often combined with re.finditer() for processing large files line by line.
— Pulling specific pieces of information (prices, dates, phone numbers) out of scraped HTML text, or cleaning inconsistent whitespace and formatting from user-submitted data.
— Validating that a password meets complexity requirements (at least one digit, one uppercase letter, minimum length) is commonly implemented with a single, carefully constructed regex pattern.

— Pulling structured values (product IDs, order numbers, currency amounts) out of free-text fields like customer support tickets or invoice descriptions, where the surrounding text varies but the pattern itself is consistent.

items.strong: 🧹 Text Preprocessing for NLP and Machine Learning
items.text: — Removing punctuation, normalising whitespace, stripping URLs or mentions from social media text, and tokenising text are all commonly handled with regex as an early preprocessing step before feeding text into ML models.

— Tools and scripts that perform bulk find-and-replace operations across many files — renaming a function consistently, updating an import path — often use regex specifically because it can match patterns, not just exact fixed strings.

— Parsing email headers, extracting all email addresses from a body of text, or pulling out specific transaction details from automated notification emails are common, practical regex applications in automation scripts.

sections.title: Why RegEx Is Worth the Genuine Learning Curve

blocks.text: Regex has a real reputation for being hard, and it's fair to acknowledge that honestly rather than pretending it's trivial. Here's why the investment still pays off:

items.text: — Unlike most Python-specific syntax, core regex knowledge transfers almost directly to JavaScript, Java, grep, sed, and dozens of other tools and languages — one of the most cross-transferable technical skills you can learn.

items.strong: 💼 It's Tested Regularly in Technical Interviews
items.text: — Writing a pattern to validate an email format, or explaining greedy versus lazy matching, are genuinely common interview questions, especially for roles involving data processing or backend validation.

items.strong: 🧹 It Genuinely Speeds Up Everyday Text Tasks
items.text: — Once the core syntax is comfortable, tasks like cleaning messy data or extracting specific fields from log files go from tedious manual string-splitting to a single confident line of code.

items.strong: 🔧 It's Foundational for Data Cleaning and NLP Work
items.text: — Nearly every real-world data science or NLP pipeline includes a text-cleaning stage that leans on regex — genuine fluency here is a practical prerequisite for that kind of work.

items.strong: 🐛 Understanding Greedy vs Lazy Prevents Silent Bugs
items.text: — This specific distinction is responsible for a genuinely large share of 'my regex ran fine but extracted the wrong thing' bugs — knowing it cold is one of the highest-value individual facts in this entire topic.

items.strong: 🇮🇳 It's a Standard Topic in Indian Data Science and Backend Interview Tracks
items.text: — Regex questions appear consistently in Indian data analyst, data science, and backend developer interview rounds, often as a practical coding exercise rather than a theory question.

— Any 'word' character: letters, digits, and underscore. \W is the opposite — any non-word character.
— Any whitespace character: space, tab, newline. \S is the opposite — any non-whitespace character.

— A capturing group versus a non-capturing group — the latter groups a pattern for repetition/alternation purposes without creating a numbered capture.
— A word boundary — matches the position between a word character and a non-word character, useful for matching whole words only.

blocks.text: These come up regularly in Python interviews, especially for data-focused and backend-validation-heavy roles.

items.q: Q1. What is the difference between re.match() and re.search() in Python?
items.a: re.match() only checks whether the pattern matches starting at the very beginning of the string — if a match exists but starts anywhere other than position zero, match() returns None. re.search() scans the entire string and returns the FIRST match found anywhere within it, regardless of position. search() is generally the more commonly needed function unless you specifically need to validate that a string begins with a certain format.

items.q: Q2. Why should regex patterns in Python usually be written as raw strings (with an r prefix)?
items.a: Regular Python strings already interpret backslash as an escape character (\n for newline, \t for tab), and regex separately uses backslash for its own special sequences (\d for digit, \b for word boundary). Without the r prefix, Python processes escape sequences first, which can silently produce a different string than intended before regex even sees the pattern — some sequences like \b collide directly with Python's own backspace escape. Writing r'\d+\b' as a raw string avoids this entirely, passing the backslashes through unmodified to the regex engine.

items.q: Q3. What is the difference between greedy and lazy (non-greedy) matching in regex?
items.a: Greedy quantifiers (*, +, {n,m}) match as MUCH text as possible while still allowing the overall pattern to succeed — this is the default behaviour. Lazy quantifiers (*?, +?, {n,m}?) match as LITTLE text as possible instead. This distinction matters most with patterns like <.+> on text containing multiple tags, where greedy matching spans from the first opening bracket all the way to the LAST closing bracket, while lazy matching correctly stops at the first closing bracket.

items.q: Q4. What does re.findall() return, and how does its behaviour change if the pattern contains capturing groups?
items.a: Without capturing groups, re.findall() returns a list of the full matched strings. If the pattern DOES contain capturing groups, findall() instead returns a list of tuples, where each tuple holds the captured groups for that match (or, if there's exactly one group, a list of just that group's matched values, without tuples).

items.q: Q5. What is a named capturing group in Python regex, and why would you use one over a numbered group?
items.a: A named group is written as (?P<name>pattern), and its matched value is retrieved via match.group('name') instead of a numeric index like match.group(1). Named groups are preferred in patterns with several groups because they make the retrieving code self-documenting and immune to breaking if the group order in the pattern later changes.

items.q: Q6. What does re.compile() do, and when is it genuinely worth using?
items.a: re.compile(pattern) parses a regex pattern once and returns a reusable Pattern object, which can then call .match(), .search(), .findall(), etc. directly. It's genuinely worth using when the same pattern will be applied repeatedly — such as inside a loop processing many lines of text — since it avoids re-parsing the same pattern string on every single call.

items.q: Q7. Why is using regex to parse full HTML or XML documents generally considered an anti-pattern?
items.a: HTML and XML have nested, recursive structure — tags inside tags, potentially arbitrarily deep — and regex is fundamentally a tool for matching patterns in flat text, not for correctly tracking nested structure. Regex-based HTML parsing tends to break on edge cases like nested identical tags, malformed markup, or comments containing tag-like text. A proper parser (like BeautifulSoup or an XML library) correctly understands the document's actual tree structure and is the appropriate tool instead.

items.q: Q8. What is the difference between re.sub() and re.subn()?
items.a: re.sub(pattern, replacement, string) returns just the new string with matches replaced. re.subn(pattern, replacement, string) returns a tuple of (new_string, number_of_substitutions_made), giving you a count of how many replacements actually occurred in addition to the resulting string itself.

blocks.text: Work through these before checking the answers. Predicting exactly what a pattern matches — including the greedy/lazy distinction — is the real test here.

items.q: 1. What does re.match(r'\d+', 'Room 42') return, and why?
items.a: None. re.match() only checks from the very START of the string. Since 'Room 42' begins with a letter, not a digit, there's no match at position 0, even though '42' does appear later in the string. re.search(r'\d+', 'Room 42') would correctly find '42'.

items.q: 2. What does re.findall(r'\d+', 'I have 3 cats and 12 dogs') return?
items.a: ['3', '12']. findall() scans the entire string and collects every non-overlapping match of one-or-more digits, returning them as a list of strings.

items.q: 3. What is the output of: re.search(r'a.c', 'abc').group()?
items.a: 'abc'. The . in regex matches any single character (except newline by default), so a.c matches 'a', any one character, then 'c' — here, the middle character happens to be 'b'.

items.q: 4. Given text = '3.14 is pi', what does re.search(r'3.14', text) actually match, and what's the subtle bug here?
items.a: It matches '3.14' correctly in this specific string, but the bug is that the . is NOT escaped, so it's actually matching ANY character in that position, not specifically a literal dot. This pattern would incorrectly also match a string like '3X14' since . matches any character. The correct, precise pattern is r'3\.14', with the dot escaped as \. to match a literal period.

items.q: 5. What does re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', 'too    many     spaces') return?
items.a: 'too many spaces'. \s+ matches one or more consecutive whitespace characters, and each such run gets replaced with a single space, effectively collapsing multiple spaces down to one.

items.q: 6. What is the output of: match = re.search(r'(\w+)@(\w+)\.com', 'reach me at admin@site.com') \n print(match.group(1), match.group(2))?
items.a: admin site. Group 1 captures the part before the @ symbol, and group 2 captures the part between @ and .com — the parentheses in the pattern define these two separate capturing groups.

items.q: 7. Why does re.findall(r'<.+>', '<a><b><c>') return ['<a><b><c>'] as a single item, not three separate tags?
items.a: Because + is greedy by default — .+ matches as much text as possible while still letting the overall pattern succeed, so it grabs everything from the very first < all the way to the very last > in the string, treating the whole thing as one match. Using the lazy version, r'<.+?>', would instead correctly return ['<a>', '<b>', '<c>'] as three separate matches.

items.q: 8. What does re.split(r'\s*,\s*', 'apple,  banana ,cherry') return?
items.a: ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']. The pattern matches a comma optionally surrounded by any amount of whitespace on either side, splitting the string at each such comma and correctly discarding the inconsistent surrounding spaces from the result.

sections.title: Conclusion — A Small Vocabulary, Genuinely Worth Learning Properly

blocks.text: Regex earns its intimidating reputation from how unreadable complex patterns can look, not from how complicated the underlying ideas actually are. A handful of special characters, a handful of core re functions, and two genuinely important distinctions — match() versus search(), and greedy versus lazy — cover the overwhelming majority of what you'll actually need for real, everyday text-processing tasks.

If you're a complete beginner, the priority is getting comfortable with the core special characters and the difference between search() and findall(), ideally by testing patterns against real, messy text rather than memorising syntax in the abstract. If you're doing real data cleaning or backend validation work, the priority shifts to precision: escaping literal characters correctly, choosing greedy versus lazy deliberately, and knowing exactly when regex is the wrong tool for a genuinely structured format like HTML or JSON.

blocks.text: The habit worth building here: whenever a pattern involves * or + and the text being matched could plausibly contain the same character or delimiter more than once, pause and specifically ask whether you actually want greedy or lazy behaviour — don't just accept the default because it's the default. That single deliberate check catches the large majority of the 'my regex ran but extracted the wrong thing' bugs before they ever ship.

Regex is a small, precise language for describing text shapes — not a mysterious black box. Learn the core vocabulary properly, respect the greedy/lazy distinction, and know when NOT to reach for it, and it becomes one of the most genuinely useful, portable tools in your entire programming toolkit. 🐍

items.q: What is RegEx in Python, and how do I use it?
items.a: RegEx (regular expressions) is a pattern language for matching and extracting text based on its shape rather than an exact fixed value. In Python, you use it through the built-in re module: import re, then call functions like re.search(pattern, text) or re.findall(pattern, text) with a pattern string (conventionally written as a raw string, with an r prefix) describing what you're looking for.

items.q: What is the difference between re.match() and re.search() in Python?
items.a: re.match() only checks whether a pattern matches starting at the very beginning of a string, returning None if a valid match exists but starts anywhere else. re.search() scans the whole string and returns the first match found anywhere within it. For most everyday tasks, search() is the more generally useful function unless you specifically need to confirm the string begins with a certain pattern.

items.q: Why do Python regex patterns usually start with an r, like r'\d+'?
items.a: The r prefix creates a raw string, which prevents Python's own string escape-sequence processing (where \n becomes a newline, for example) from interfering with regex's separate use of backslashes for its own special sequences like \d or \b. Without the raw string prefix, certain regex patterns can be silently altered by Python before the regex engine ever receives them, so writing patterns as raw strings is the standard, safe convention.

items.q: What is the difference between greedy and lazy matching in regex?
items.a: Greedy quantifiers like * and + match as much text as possible while still letting the overall pattern succeed — this is the default behaviour in Python regex. Lazy (non-greedy) quantifiers, written with a ? added after them (*?, +?), match as little text as possible instead. This distinction matters most when a pattern could span multiple similar delimiters in the target text, where greedy matching often grabs far more than intended.

items.q: What are capturing groups in Python regex, and how do I use them?
items.a: Capturing groups are created by wrapping part of a pattern in parentheses, like (\d{4}) to capture a four-digit year specifically. After a successful match, match.group(1) retrieves the first captured group's text, match.group(2) the second, and so on — or match.groups() returns all captured groups together as a tuple. Named groups, written as (?P<name>pattern), let you retrieve them more readably via match.group('name') instead of a numeric index.

items.q: Should I use regex to parse HTML or JSON in Python?
items.a: No — this is a well-known anti-pattern. HTML, XML, and JSON have nested, recursive structure that regex isn't designed to reliably handle, since it fundamentally matches flat patterns rather than tracking nested structure. Use a proper parsing library instead — BeautifulSoup or an XML parser for HTML/XML, and Python's built-in json module for JSON — and reserve regex for genuinely flat, pattern-based text matching.
